questions.question: A car's speedometer shows 60 km/h at one instant. How does this instant rate relate to the average rate over a journey, and what is the mathematical link?
questions.solution: Average rate = total distance/total time (a secant slope). The speedometer shows the limit of average rates as the time interval shrinks to zero — the TANGENT slope, f′(t). The derivative is defined as lim(h→0)[f(t+h) − f(t)]/h: the average rate's limit, not a different quantity.

questions.question: If y depends on u and u depends on x, why does dy/dx = dy/du · du/dx? Frame it as a rate question.
questions.solution: Rates MULTIPLY along a chain: if y changes 3 units per unit of u, and u changes 2 units per unit of x, then y changes 3×2 = 6 per unit of x. The Leibniz notation makes the cancellation visually suggestive (du appears in both fractions) — the rigorous content is that the composed difference quotient factors. This is why substitution works and related-rates problems multiply rates.

questions.concept: First derivative test vs second derivative test
questions.question: f′(c) = 0 tells you c is critical. What does f″ tell you, and when does the second derivative test FAIL?
questions.solution: f″(c) > 0 → local minimum (concave up); f″(c) < 0 → local maximum (concave down). If f″(c) = 0 the test is INCONCLUSIVE — e.g. x³ has f′(0) = f″(0) = 0 but no extremum (an inflection point), while x⁴ has a minimum. Then fall back to the first-derivative sign change across c. Knowing when the shortcut breaks is the tested understanding.

questions.concept: Increasing/decreasing from the sign of f′
questions.question: Why does f′(x) > 0 on an interval guarantee f is increasing there, geometrically?
questions.solution: f′ is the tangent slope; if every tangent on the interval points upward, the function cannot fall between any two points (by the Mean Value Theorem, f(b) − f(a) = f′(c)(b−a) > 0). The MVT converts a local statement (positive slopes) into a global one (monotone increase) — that bridge is the reason the sign test is valid.

questions.concept: Maxima in word problems — the constraint
questions.question: A farmer fences a rectangular field with 100 m of wire against a river (no fence needed on the river side). Why is the maximum-area rectangle NOT a square here?
questions.solution: Constraint: 2x + y = 100 → y = 100 − 2x. Area A = x(100−2x) = 100x − 2x², maximised at x = 25, y = 50 — the field is 1:2, not 1:1. The river side removes one fence, changing the constraint; the unconstrained-perimeter optimum (square) no longer applies. ALWAYS write the constraint first — the constraint determines the shape of the optimum.

questions.concept: Related rates — differentiating the relation, not the numbers
questions.question: A spherical balloon inflates at 10 cm³/s. Why must you differentiate V = (4/3)πr³ with respect to TIME, not just differentiate and plug in?
questions.solution: dV/dt = 4πr²·dr/dt — both V and r are functions of time, so the chain rule produces the r²·dr/dt factor. Substituting the INSTANT value of r gives the instant dr/dt. The error to avoid: differentiating as if r were constant. Every related-rates problem is a chain-rule problem in disguise.

questions.concept: Tangent and normal — the two lines
questions.question: At a point on y = x², the tangent has slope 4. What is the slope of the normal there, and why is the product of the two slopes −1?
questions.solution: Normal slope = −1/4. Two lines are perpendicular iff m₁·m₂ = −1 (the rotation by 90° inverts and negates the slope). Tangent slope comes from the derivative; the normal is its negative reciprocal — both are needed for distance-from-curve problems.

questions.question: Use differentials to estimate √25.3 without a calculator, and state why the estimate is slightly off in a predictable direction.
questions.solution: f(x) = √x, f′ = 1/(2√x). At a = 25: f(25.3) ≈ 5 + 0.3·(1/10) = 5.03. The linear (tangent) approximation OVERESTIMATES here because √x is concave — the tangent lies above the curve. Concavity determines the error's sign; the differential is the first-order term of the Taylor expansion.
